issues.legal_issue: Amounts receivable as arrears of rent and royalty that are acquired as assigned rights are not taxable as income merely because they are collected by the purchaser.
material_facts: The company acquired proprietary interests in leased lands under conveyances that also assigned the former owner's right to receive rent and royalty arrears.

The arrears related to a period before the conveyances, and the company became entitled to them under the conveyances as purchaser of those rights, not as owner of the lands during the period in which they accrued.
The tax authorities assessed the arrears as the company's income.
issues.conclusion: The arrears were not assessable as the company's income.
issues.legal_principle: The tax character of a receipt depends on the nature of the right acquired. Arrears acquired under a conveyance as a purchased right to collect them are not income of the purchaser merely because the purchaser later receives them; the fact that the arrears were not taken into account in setting the conveyance price does not alter the character of the acquired right. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.

predicates.arrears_assessed_as_income: In an income-tax assessment, amounts receivable as arrears of rent or royalty were treated as the recipient's income.
predicates.arrears_acquired_by_assignment_as_purcha: The recipient acquired the right to collect the arrears by purchasing that right under a conveyance.
predicates.arrears_not_accrued_to_purchaser_as_owne: The arrears related to a period when the recipient did not own the property and the right to them did not arise from ownership during that period.

issues.definition: When arrears are assessed as income but were acquired as a purchaser's assigned right and did not accrue to the purchaser as owner, the rule treats them as not taxable income.

issues.legal_issue: A profitable resale of property does not establish that its acquisition and sale were a trading adventure when the surrounding facts do not rationally support that inference.
material_facts: The company said it acquired mining properties to develop mines but sold them because it lacked finance.
The company was heavily indebted to the vendor, but there was no evidence that the vendor pressed for payment.
Its memorandum of association authorized it to acquire, sell, dispose of, and deal with mining properties, but there was no evidence that it had acquired or sold other properties.
Other mining companies occupied a major part of the acquired lands, making large-scale profitable mining by the company impracticable.
The company resold the properties soon after acquiring them and made a profit.
The tax authorities treated the resale profit as business income, relying on the transaction as a trading adventure.
issues.conclusion: The facts found by the Tribunal did not support the conclusion that the acquisition and resale were a trading adventure, so the profit was not assessable as business income on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Whether an isolated transaction is a trading adventure is determined from the evidentiary facts, and a profit, prompt resale, corporate authority to deal in such property, or inability to conduct profitable operations does not by itself establish that the transaction was carried out in the course of business. The Court applied the approach to trading adventures in G. Venkataswami Naidu and Co. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, 35 I.T.R. 594.

rule.if: income_tax_assessment_of_property_resale and property_resold_at_profit and (corporate_authority_to_deal_in_property or prompt_resale or mining_unprofitable_or_impracticable) and no_other_property_dealings_shown and facts_do_not_support_trade_inference

predicates.income_tax_assessment_of_property_resale: An income-tax assessment treats profit from a property's resale as business income on the ground that the transaction was a trading adventure.
predicates.property_resold_at_profit: The property was resold for more than its acquisition cost.
predicates.corporate_authority_to_deal_in_property: The entity's governing documents authorize it to acquire, sell, dispose of, or deal in that kind of property.
predicates.prompt_resale: The property was sold soon after it was acquired.
predicates.mining_unprofitable_or_impracticable: The entity could not undertake large-scale profitable mining on the acquired land.
predicates.no_other_property_dealings_shown: There is no evidence that the entity acquired or sold other properties in the course of similar dealings.
predicates.facts_do_not_support_trade_inference: The primary facts, considered individually or together, provide no rational basis for inferring that the acquisition and resale were a trading adventure.

issues.definition: When a profitable property resale is assessed as a trading adventure, but the listed indications and the other evidence do not rationally support a trade inference, the profit is not assessable as business income on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: A factual inference drawn by a tax tribunal from primary facts may be examined in a reference proceeding when it lacks legal evidentiary support or is not rationally possible.
material_facts: The Tribunal inferred from the primary facts that the company's acquisition and resale of mining properties were in the course of business.
The High Court examined whether that inference was supported by the primary facts and concluded that it was not.
The matter came before the High Court by reference from the Tribunal under the income-tax law.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in examining the correctness of the Tribunal's inference.
issues.legal_principle: Under the approach stated in G. Venkataswami Naidu and Co. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, 35 I.T.R. 594, a factual conclusion based on an inference from proved primary facts can be challenged in reference proceedings within narrow limits: a party may contend that it is unsupported by legal evidence or is not rationally possible. If that contention is established, the court considers whether the conclusion is perverse and should be set aside.

predicates.tax_reference_proceeding: The matter is before a High Court in a reference proceeding concerning a tax tribunal's decision.
predicates.tribunal_inferred_conclusion_from_primar: The tribunal drew a factual conclusion by inference from primary evidentiary facts.
predicates.inference_unsupported_by_legal_evidence: The inferred conclusion lacks support in legal evidence.
predicates.inference_not_rationally_possible: The inferred conclusion cannot rationally be drawn from the relevant facts.

issues.definition: In a tax reference, a High Court may review a tribunal's inferred factual conclusion when the inference lacks legal evidentiary support or is not rationally possible.
